**Team X · Solar farms and nearby home values in upstate New York**\
Ana Torres, Ben Mwangi, Carla Novak, Dev Raman, Eva Lindqvist

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}

are real. It asks a question a town would act on. The [Target

## 1. Research question

Does a new solar farm lower the sale prices of homes within one
kilometer of it in upstate New York? This is an evaluation. A town
planning board reviewing a solar farm would act on the answer. New
York leaves farms under 25 megawatts to local approval, so towns
approve most of the state's solar farms (New York State Department of
Public Service, n.d.). We expect prices within one kilometer to fall by
1 to 3 percent after the farm begins operating, relative to homes 2 to
5 kilometers from the same farm. We are wrong if prices near and far
move together after the farm opens.

## 2. Why it matters

The planning board decides how far the panels must sit from homes and
whether the developer must screen them with trees. If nearby homes lose
value, the board can set the setback at the distance where the loss
fades, and require screening inside it. If they lose nothing, a longer
setback takes land from the project and costs the town the farm's tax
payments for no gain.

Two studies come closest to ours. Elmallah et al. (2023) studied more
than 1,500 projects in six states. Homes within half a mile sold for
about 1.5 percent less than homes two to four miles away, and the effect
was not measurable beyond one mile. Gaur and Lang (2023) found that
homes within 0.6 miles in Massachusetts and Rhode Island lost 1.5 to 3.6
percent of their value after a farm was built, mostly where the farm
replaced farmland or forest in rural areas. We add evidence from upstate
New York, where towns approve the farms. In 20 towns we also test
whether prices moved when the farm was approved, before it was built.

## 3. Approach

Each observation is one sale of a single-family home. The outcome is
the logarithm of the sale price, from the ATTOM sales records in Dewey.
The sample covers sales from 2012 to 2025 within 5 kilometers of the
431 farms of 1 to 25 megawatts that began operating in upstate New York
between 2016 and 2023. Upstate here means outside New York City, Long
Island, Westchester and Rockland. These are the farms that town
planning boards decide on.

The treatment is a solar farm beginning operation within 1 kilometer of
the home before it sells. Prices may already move when the board
approves a farm, so we leave out sales in the two years before each farm
opens. The comparison group is the sales of homes 2 to 5 kilometers from
the same farm in the same years. Their prices stand in for the
counterfactual, what prices within 1 kilometer would have done without
the farm. We leave out homes between 1 and 2 kilometers, which may be
partly affected. The design is difference-in-differences. It compares
the change in prices near each farm, from before it opened to after,
with the change farther away. Farms open in different years, so we date
each sale by the years before or after its own farm opened and estimate
the effect year by year, which is an event study. The identifying
assumption is that, without the farm, prices within 1 kilometer would
have followed the same trend as prices 2 to 5 kilometers away.

In the 20 towns with the most farms, we also collect the date the
planning board approved each farm from the board's minutes. We use
those dates to test whether prices moved at approval.

## 4. Data and access

| Dataset | Holder | Unit and period | Variables we need | Access time | Status |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Real Estate Transaction Data (ATTOM) | Dewey, through Cornell's subscription | Sale, 2012–2025 | Price, date, location, size, year built, property type | Days | File opened Oct 16 |
| U.S. Large-Scale Solar Photovoltaic Database, version 4.0 | U.S. Geological Survey and Berkeley Lab, public | Farm, operating through 2025 | Outline, capacity, first year of operation | Now | File opened Oct 12 |
| Planning board minutes | Town clerks, public | Board meeting | Date each farm was approved | Weeks | Holder contacted Oct 15, for 3 of 20 towns |

We expect to hold all three by November 30. If the approval dates have
not arrived by then, we drop the approval test, and the question
narrows to the effect of a farm once it operates.

Property records can identify owners, so we cannot rule out IRB review
ourselves. We asked the IRB office to decide on September 18. On
October 7 it asked which fields we keep, and we answered that we drop
owner names when we load the file. We expect its determination by
mid-November. If it asks for an application, that is our slowest
approval, and it has to start by November 18. We need no data-use
agreement, because we have no sponsor and every source is public or
covered by Cornell's Dewey subscription.

## 5. Anticipated challenges

The main threat is selection into treatment, through where each farm
sits. Developers choose cheap, flat land near power lines, often
farmland at the edge of a village. Prices within 1 kilometer of that
land may already have been growing more slowly than prices 2 to 5
kilometers away, closer to the village. The near ring would then lag
the far ring for reasons unrelated to the farm, which pushes our
estimate toward a larger loss. We cannot measure the developer's choice
of parcel, but the event study shows whether near and far prices
drifted apart before the farm opened. If they did, we will report by
February 15, the date we set for first estimates, that the design
cannot separate the farm from the place.

The approval dates are the row of our resource map most likely to stop
us. Three of the 20 town clerks have answered, and older minutes may
exist only on paper. Eva writes to the other 17 by October 30. If fewer
than 15 towns have sent dates by November 30, we drop the approval
test, as in our plan B, and record the change in our decision log.

Shedding light on large-scale solar impacts: An analysis of property

utility-scale solar arrays on housing prices. *Energy Economics* 122:
106699. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eneco.2023.106699>
